'''Elizabeth Essex-Cohen''' ({{nee}} '''Elizabeth Annette Essex'''; 21 April 1940 – 21 March 2004) was an Australian physicist who worked in [[global positioning satellite]] physics and was among the first women in Australia to be awarded a PhD in physics.

== Early life and education ==
Elizabeth Annette Essex was educated at [[Grafton High School (New South Wales)|Grafton High]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=|first=|date=2017-08-05|title=Fitting tribute to true pioneer of space science|work=Daily Telegraph|url=https://www.newsregionalmedia.com.au/news/fitting-tribute-to-true-pioneer-of-space-science/news-story/de9b6be5c21f1d8416d044882ed2e4d3|access-date=2021-11-26}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> She subsequently completed a PhD in physics at Australia's [[University of New England (Australia)|University of New England]], investigating [[Ionosphere|ionospheric]] irregularities under Frank Hibberd, graduating in 1966.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Elizabeth  A. Essex-Cohen Ionospheric Physics Papers etc|url=http://harveycohen.net/essex/|access-date=2021-11-26|website=harveycohen.net}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|volume =50|issue=2|page=71|journal=Australian Physics|title=Obituary:Frank Hibberd|url=https://physics.org.au/wp-content/uploads/Australian%20Physics/Aust%20Phys%2050-2.pdf|access-date=2021-11-26}}</ref> Essex-Cohen was the fourth woman in Australia to receive a [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in physics.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=University|first=La Trobe|title=Elizabeth Essex-Cohen (nee Essex)|url=https://www.latrobe.edu.au/about/vision/diversity-and-inclusion/square-the-ledger/profiles/elizabeth-essex-cohen-nee-essex|access-date=2021-11-26|website=www.latrobe.edu.au|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|last=Centre|first=The University of Melbourne eScholarship Research|title=Essex-Cohen, Elizabeth Annette - Bright Sparcs Biographical entry|url=https://www.asap.unimelb.edu.au/bsparcs/biogs/P004560b.htm|access-date=2021-11-26|website=www.asap.unimelb.edu.au|language=en-gb}}</ref>

== Career and impact ==
After graduating her PhD, Essex-Cohen worked at [[University of the West Indies]] and [[James Cook University]] before taking up a lectureship position in [[space physics]] at [[La Trobe University]] in 1968.<ref name=":3" /> She remained at La Trobe for the remainder of her career, though in 1974 and 1978/9 she had simultaneous positions at the US Air Force Geophysics Laboratory as part of her [[Global Positioning System|GPS]] research.<ref name=":3" /> Her initial work focused on the use of [[Radio propagation|radio wave reflection]] to study irregularities in the [[ionosphere]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|last=Lapps|first=By|date=2017-08-05|title=Ionospheric scientist helped shape GPS|work=Daily Telegraph|url=https://www.newsregionalmedia.com.au/news/ionospheric-scientist-helped-shape-gps/news-story/437de360d1df0903288f43c7dab2322c|access-date=2021-11-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=|title=Fitting tribute to true pioneer of space science|url=https://www.qt.com.au/news/fitting-tribute-to-true-pioneer-of-space-science/3209173/|url-status=dead|access-date=2021-04-14|website=Queensland Times|language=en|archive-date=2021-04-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414041129/https://www.qt.com.au/news/fitting-tribute-to-true-pioneer-of-space-science/3209173/}}</ref>

Her work on radio transmission through the ionosphere led to some of her best-known work in communications between ground and satellites. In the early US Air force's development of GPS (then called Navstar), she was the only Australian involved in the design. Her collaborations with [[Australian Antarctic Division]] and the [[Cooperative Research Centre#Information Technology and communication technology|Co-operative Research Centre for Satellite Systems]] led to her having a significant role in the development of Australia's [[FedSat]] satellite (active 2002-2007<ref>{{Cite web|last=Macey|first=Richard|date=2007-09-28|title=A beacon of hope falls silent|url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/a-beacon-of-hope-falls-silent-20070928-gdr7r4.html|access-date=2021-11-26|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}}</ref>).<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Centre|first=The University of Melbourne eScholarship Research|title=Essex-Cohen, Elizabeth Annette - Biographical entry - Encyclopedia of Australian Science|url=https://www.eoas.info/biogs/P004560b.htm|access-date=2021-11-26|website=www.eoas.info|language=en-gb}}</ref>

== Death ==
Essex-Cohen became hospitalised for [[mesothelioma]] in December 2002. After a brief remission which enabled her to attend a Wireless Science conference, she died on 21 March 2004, aged 63. Tributes included a special session of the (International) Beacon Satellite Group.<ref name=":0" />
